segments.narration: This 9,000-year-old town had no streets at all. Southern Turkey, on the Konya Plain. No lanes, no doors at ground level. People came and went across the rooftops.
Houses packed wall to wall in a honeycomb. You dropped in through a hole in the ceiling, which was also the chimney.
And the dead stayed home. They lie in pits under the floors, beneath the hearths and sleeping platforms. The earliest graves hold close relatives.
Eighteen levels of this stack up. Each house rebuilt on the flattened one below it, for roughly fifteen hundred years.
Genetics published in 2025 points to homes handed down from mother to daughter. A town laid out by who you were related to, not by roads.

verdicts.claim: Çatalhöyük, on the Konya Plain in southern Anatolia, Turkey, had no footpaths or streets between its dwellings, and its rooftops served as its streets.
verdicts.note: 100% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: The houses were packed together in a honeycomb-like maze and most were entered through holes in the ceiling, which were also the only ventilation for hearth and oven smoke.
verdicts.note: 88% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: The dead at Çatalhöyük were buried in pits beneath house floors, especially under hearths, platforms and beds, and early burials were of closely related families.
verdicts.note: 100% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article

verdicts.claim: As many as eighteen levels of settlement have been uncovered at Çatalhöyük, which was occupied from about 7100 BC to about 5600 BC.
verdicts.note: Wikipedia gives as many as eighteen levels of settlement and an occupation of about 7100 BC to about 5600 BC, roughly fifteen hundred years; the article's lead gives a wider 7500-5600 BC span, so the narration uses the conservative figure.

verdicts.claim: A 2025 genetic study of Çatalhöyük suggests early matrilocality and matrilineality, with households passing from mother to daughter.
verdicts.note: 91% of the claim's wording appears in the reference article, including 1 number(s)
